response.consequence: Traces with very deep span parent chains (more than about 1000 levels) can be flushed as several fragmented segments. This is a rare case.
response.explanation: The loop bound in add-buffer.lua went from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000`. The old comment said the limit meant segment trees deeper than 10k might not join correctly. With 1000, a parent chain of more than about 1000 redirects ends the loop before reaching the real root set. `set_span_id` is then an intermediate span, and the span is merged into the wrong set key. The segment is split, so later spans can land in a different set from the rest of the segment.
response.title: Redirect-chain traversal limit cut from 10000 to 1000

response.consequence: An admin request to the audit log endpoint with optimized_pagination=true and a negative-offset cursor fails with an unhandled AssertionError, which returns a 500. The advertised negative-offset feature does not work. The unreachable-by-design branch also gives a misleading security and performance claim ("access to data beyond normal pagination bounds").
response.explanation: When enable_advanced_features is true and cursor.offset < 0, get_result runs queryset[cursor.offset:stop]. The comment says Django handles negative slicing. It does not: QuerySet.__getitem__ asserts that negative indexing is not supported. The audit log endpoint passes enable_advanced_features=True whenever optimized_pagination=true and the user is a superuser or has global access. A client-supplied cursor with a negative offset, such as "0:-5:1", therefore reaches this branch. The change also adds no validation that rejects such offsets. If it did slice, the result would be wrong anyway, because the stop bound would be the sum of a negative start and the limit.
response.title: Negative-offset path slices the queryset with a negative start, which Django rejects
